clinicalPearls: Menopause is the permanent cessation of menstruation from loss of ovarian follicular function and is diagnosed retrospectively after 12 months of amenorrhea; the average age in U.S. women is about 51 years.

Perimenopause is the transition preceding menopause when fertility wanes and cycles become irregular, typically beginning 2-8 years before the final menses (mean duration about 4 years); smoking advances the transition by roughly 2 years.

Perimenopause is marked by 'irregularly irregular' hormone levels rather than the consistently high FSH and low estradiol of established menopause; intermenstrual intervals often shorten (by about 3 days) due to an accelerated follicular phase.

FSH rises before LH during the transition, attributed to loss of inhibin and estrogen feedback; after menopause estradiol falls markedly while estrone is relatively preserved through peripheral aromatization of adrenal and ovarian androgens.

Vasomotor symptoms (hot flashes, night sweats), irregular bleeding, and vaginal dryness are strongly attributable to the transition; sleep disturbance has moderate supporting evidence, while mood swings, memory/concentration changes, incontinence, and sexual dysfunction are not clearly caused by ovarian aging alone.
Nearly 60% of women in one U.S. study reported hot flashes in the 2 years before their final menses; symptom intensity, frequency, duration, and quality-of-life impact are highly variable.
Estrogen therapy is the most effective treatment for vasomotor and genitourinary symptoms; randomized trial data suggest hormone therapy reduces menopausal symptoms by roughly 65-90%.

The 'timing hypothesis' holds that estrogen may slow early atherosclerosis but adversely affect advanced lesions, so women initiating hormone therapy early after menopause may differ in cardiovascular outcome from those starting many years later.
Primary prevention of cardiovascular disease should NOT be considered an expected benefit of hormone therapy; an increased stroke risk and a small early increase in coronary risk should be weighed.
A 1-year absence of spontaneous menses reliably indicates ovulation has ceased, but natural menstrual pattern cannot be assessed while a woman is taking oral contraceptives.

Estrogen reduces bone turnover and resorption; postmenopausal estrogen (with or without a progestogen) increases spine bone density by about 4-6% and hip density by about 2-3%, with WHI showing roughly a 33% reduction in hip fractures.

Unopposed estrogen markedly raises endometrial cancer risk; adding a progestogen opposes this effect and can even reduce endometrial cancer risk, which is why estrogen-only therapy is reserved for women without a uterus.
harrison.pathophysiology: Ovarian mass and fertility decline sharply after age 35 and more steeply during perimenopause as the pool of primary follicles, depleting since before birth, runs down. Altered folliculogenesis and reduced inhibin secretion cause FSH to rise; the propensity for anovulatory cycles produces a relatively hyperestrogenic, hypoprogestagenic milieu that may underlie the increased perimenopausal incidence of endometrial hyperplasia/carcinoma, uterine polyps, and leiomyomata. With transition into menopause, estradiol falls markedly while estrone is comparatively preserved through peripheral aromatization of adrenal and ovarian androgens; FSH rises more than LH owing to loss of inhibin plus estrogen feedback. Exogenous estrogen lowers LDL and raises HDL cholesterol by about 10-15% and favorably affects lipoprotein(a), LDL oxidation, and endothelial function, but it also raises triglycerides, promotes coagulation (factor VII, prothrombin fragments, fibrinopeptide A), and elevates C-reactive protein, providing a mechanistic basis for both potential benefits and thrombotic/inflammatory harms.
additionalDifferentials: Pregnancy as a cause of amenorrhea in perimenopausal women (unintentional pregnancy rate in the forties rivals that of adolescents)
Premature ovarian insufficiency / primary ovarian insufficiency when ovarian failure occurs well before the usual age
Thyroid dysfunction or other endocrine causes of menstrual irregularity and vasomotor-like symptoms
Uterine structural lesions (leiomyomata, endometrial polyps, hyperplasia or carcinoma) presenting as abnormal/heavy bleeding
Other age-related conditions causing midlife mood, sleep, cognitive, or sexual complaints not attributable to ovarian senescence
nonInfectiousMimics: Thyroid disease producing vasomotor-like flushing and menstrual change
Anxiety or panic disorder mimicking hot flashes
Endometrial hyperplasia or carcinoma presenting as abnormal bleeding rather than physiologic transition
Medication effects or other causes of secondary amenorrhea
additionalInvestigations: Menstrual cycle history as the principal STRAW+10 criterion for staging reproductive aging, with biomarkers as supportive criteria
FSH measurement: random level >25 IU/L is characteristic of the late menopausal transition; day-3 levels <20, 20 to <30, and >=30 IU/L indicate good, fair, and poor pregnancy likelihood respectively
Estradiol levels, recognizing that FSH and estradiol are imperfect diagnostic indicators in still-menstruating perimenopausal women due to marked intraindividual variability
Anti-mullerian hormone and inhibin B as additional markers of reproductive aging
Transvaginal ultrasound (with saline enhancement) to detect leiomyomata or polyps when bleeding is abnormal
Endometrial aspiration/biopsy to identify hyperplastic or premalignant changes when menorrhagia or abnormal bleeding occurs
Bone mineral density assessment and FRAX 10-year fracture risk estimation to guide osteoporosis decisions; 25-hydroxyvitamin D level >=50 nmol/L considered sufficient for bone maintenance
redFlags: Unexplained or undiagnosed vaginal bleeding requires evaluation to exclude endometrial hyperplasia or carcinoma before attributing it to the transition
An acute coronary event or stroke while on hormone therapy mandates immediate discontinuation of therapy
New or worsening vasomotor symptoms accompanied by features suggesting thromboembolism, given the increased VTE risk with oral estrogen
Heavy menstrual bleeding (menorrhagia) in perimenopause warrants evaluation for uterine disorders rather than assumption of benign cause
Symptoms or signs of estrogen-dependent malignancy in a woman considering or using hormone therapy
harrison.prognosis: Most peri- and postmenopausal symptoms are self-limited though variable in duration and intensity. In the WHI, many risks and benefits of hormone therapy dissipated within 5-7 years after stopping, though some persisted: with estrogen-progestin an elevated breast cancer risk continued over long follow-up and a reduced hip fracture risk and reduced endometrial cancer risk persisted; with estrogen alone the breast cancer risk reduction became significant on extended follow-up. Estrogen-progestin carried an overall unfavorable global benefit-risk profile that did not vary by 10-year age group, whereas estrogen-only therapy had a roughly neutral profile overall with a more favorable balance in younger women (relative risks for the global index of about 0.84, 0.99, and 1.17 in ages 50-59, 60-69, and 70-79). Over extended follow-up estrogen alone was associated with reduced all-cause mortality in women aged 50-59 (notably those with bilateral oophorectomy), while estrogen-progestin showed elevated breast cancer risk and a suggestion of increased breast cancer mortality.
pitfalls: Observational studies overstated cardiovascular benefit because women choosing hormone therapy tend to be healthier and more health-conscious (healthy-user confounding); randomized trials did not confirm the benefit.
Relying on a single FSH or estradiol value to diagnose perimenopause in a menstruating woman is unreliable given extreme intraindividual variability.
Prescribing unopposed estrogen to a woman with an intact uterus markedly raises endometrial cancer and atypical hyperplasia risk; a progestogen is needed for endometrial protection.
Attributing midlife mood, cognitive, urinary, or sexual complaints to menopause when evidence does not support ovarian aging as the principal cause.
Counseling should emphasize absolute rather than relative risk measures, since absolute risks rise with age even when relative risks are similar.
Apparent excess breast cancer detection in early hormone therapy users may partly reflect more frequent screening mammography rather than a true biologic effect.
Assuming the cardiovascular and other effects of one formulation/route apply to all, since transdermal estrogen may carry lower thrombotic and gallbladder risk than oral estrogen.
harrison.severityClassification: The Stages of Reproductive Aging Workshop +10 (STRAW+10) system stages reproductive aging using menstrual cycle characteristics as principal criteria (e.g., persistent >=7-day differences in consecutive cycle length in the early transition; an interval of amenorrhea of >=60 days in the late transition) with endocrine markers (FSH, AMH, inhibin B, antral follicle count) as supportive criteria, spanning reproductive, menopausal transition (perimenopause), and postmenopause stages around the final menstrual period.
management: Systemic menopausal hormone therapy with oestrogen, combined with a progestogen when the uterus is intact, as the most effective treatment for vasomotor symptoms
Low-dose vaginal oestrogen for genitourinary syndrome of menopause and vaginal dryness
Non-hormonal alternatives such as SSRIs or SNRIs, gabapentin, clonidine or a neurokinin-3 receptor antagonist for women who cannot or prefer not to take hormones
Individualised shared decision-making that weighs breast cancer and venous thromboembolism risk, favouring transdermal oestrogen where thrombotic risk is a concern
Bone protection with weight-bearing exercise, calcium and vitamin D, and antiresorptive therapy such as bisphosphonates for osteoporosis
Cardiovascular risk factor optimisation and lifestyle measures including smoking cessation
Endometrial assessment for abnormal or unscheduled bleeding, with periodic review of the ongoing need for hormone therapy
